.NEAR TERM...
(Rest of today and tonight)
Issued at 122 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

Other than the breezy south winds, pleasant weather conditions are 
continue this afternoon, with highs in the 60's to low-70s and 
scattered high clouds. Winds diminish with sunset and temperatures
decrease into the 40's overnight. Patchy fog development remains 
possible on Thursday morning, particularly across southern and far
western Oklahoma and portions of western north Texas.

Thompson

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Thursday through Friday night)
Issued at 122 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

Increasing temperatures and low-level moisture are expected 
through the short term period with persistent return flow. Winds 
will be less breezy on Thursday as the upper trough ejects from 
the northern plains ahead of a low-amplitude ridge. Guidance
continues to suggest patchy fog on Friday morning though coverage
remains uncertain.

Another strong upper trough moves reaches the Great Basin by 
Friday morning. As the H500 jet translates from the four corners 
region towards the north-central plains, the surface pressure 
gradient tightens with the deepening of another quick- moving mid-
latitude cyclone. This will instigate another day of breezy south
winds across the area, with sustained winds at 15 to 25 mph and
gusts of 30 to 40 mph concentrated across northwest, northern, and
west-central Oklahoma. Gusts to 25 mph will extend across southwest
Oklahoma and adjacent north Texas, as well.

Thompson

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Saturday through Tuesday)
Issued at 1250 AM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

We continue to closely monitor a weekend weather system, expected
to bring cooler temperatures and chances for rain/thunderstorms. 
The initially coherent upper wave across the Great Basin 
continues to trend towards becoming "strung out"/sheared with time
into Saturday. 

The more interesting model trend over the past 24 hours has been 
the emergent depiction of a trailing vorticity maxima rounding the
base of the broader trough across the Four Corners into the 
Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles by Saturday evening. With a more direct 
shot of synoptic forcing, and more notable/stronger surface 
reflection, chances for rain & storms are back on the rise on 
Saturday and Saturday night, both ahead of and along/near the 
approaching surface front. 

In terms of impact(s) brought by this activity, lightning looks to  
be the primary concern, with very limited instability (due to 
meager moisture return & warm mid-level temperatures) precluding 
a risk for strong-severe storms. "Most likely" rainfall totals 
(up to a few tenths) also don't point towards much in the way of 
hydrologic concern as of now.

As a surface low rapidly advances northeastward into the Central 
Plains, a cold front will begin to shove southeastward across the 
area. The modified post-frontal airmass still looks to be 
relatively modest (i.e., less cold) by late November standards, 
though a cooldown by upwards of 10-15 degrees remains likely into 
Sunday across the area.

Another storm system looks poised to impact the region on Monday 
into Tuesday, bringing additional chances for rain/storms and a 
reinforcement to cooler temperatures.

Ungar

&&

.AVIATION...
(00Z TAFS)
Issued at 442 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

South winds will diminish quickly this evening with mainly clear
skies. Late tonight we could see some patchy fog that could impact
parts of the area and have maintained a mention at several sites,
including DUA/SPS/LAW/CSM/WWR. This should dissipate fairly
quickly after sunrise. South winds will be around 10-15kts with
some gusts over 20kts across the west by late morning.
